en: Badisha’s Akshunkar
Is entrusted to you, boys.
If the noble falcon remains safe
And you bring it before my eyes,
If you return safely to me,
I shall agree to what you ask:
From among the slender beauties
In red dresses and crescent belts,
I shall obtain wives for you!
If you make these words of mine come true,
For the twin boys that you are,
Your poor sister-in-law Chachykey
Would sacrifice her very life!”
Your sister-in-law said this in sorrow,
Raised her voice and uttered her lament.
Semetey, the son of Manas,
Wore out horses and ranged the land;
Would that blue-maned champion heed her?
He loosed his hounds and flew his birds,
Taking fourteen swift horses,
And the two choros who followed him.
Your prince mounted in high spirits,
Crossed ridge after ridge,
And passed over broken, mottled ground.
At Jangyryk’s Jar-Kyya,
Along the winding single track,
The bloodthirsty one now arrived.
At the mouth of that ravine
A mass of white fiber lay like a band of dawn;
Your noble prince now saw it
And turned Buurul’s head toward it.
He rejoiced when he saw the fiber,
Turned toward Kanchoro and Kulchoro,
And joyfully spoke to the two:
“Kulchoro and Kanchoro—
You two are companions alike to me,
My bright stars in the sky,
The sable trim upon my collar,
My steeds that could carry me six months,
You who kicked together like foals,
Who struggled for the same breast,
My two brothers, alike in every way.
If we see the many Black Chinese and Manchu hosts,
They will seem a swarm of black worms;
If we are caught together on campaign,
Firing guns and drawing bows,
If we stand and fight without fleeing,
If we confront them face to face,
If a night of painful hardship falls
And we meet in bitter battle,
We shall need armor to wear in the struggle.
This white fiber we have found
Could be of great use to us, if you agree.”
From my magnanimous father Manas,
The Akolpok left to me as an heirloom
Has had its fiber plucked away;
The six bastards, Abyke and Köbösh,
Have worn it bare like this.
It has come to us by providence—
Look, boys!
We have found white fiber.
For the colt one means to favor,
The road is made ready;
For the colt one means to deny,
No fiber comes even when he buys it.
Let us take the fiber in the field
As our rightful spoil.
My valiant mother Kanykey’s
Stripped and ruined Akolpok—
Let us have it fitted out once more.
There are many places to scout,
And many peoples who may clash with us.
Think carefully, boys:
There are Russians on the lowland side,
Chinese along the ridges,
And muskets before our brows;
Many foes may contend with us.”
When your hero had said this,
Kulchoro flew like an arrow
And went toward the fiber.
Then he remembered the words
Of your delicate sister-in-law.
His sister-in-law had said:
“If fiber is found among the spoils,
Do not even glance at it.”
The one about to abandon the fiber
Was Almambet’s son;
But would the road allow it?
He swept it together and seized it.
At the bottom of a great cave
He piled it all together,
And with a black stone as large as a house,
That tiger-natured boy
Closed and sealed it securely.
The horse beneath him was
Abyke’s Aktelki;
Kulchoro spurred it forward
And quickly caught up again.
When the magnanimous sultan came
Along the shore of Ala-Köl,
How wondrous Ala-Köl proved to be!
Its giant hogweed was thick as an arm;
When you looked at its maral deer,
They were like pale, white-faced cows.
Its apples ripened till the valley was broad with them;
Its walnuts fell and filled the ravines.
Its cuckoo sang among the willows;
Its laughing nightingales and sparrows
Talked together in the willow tops.
Its keskelidirik were like puppies,
And its wild asses like yearling colts;
When you looked at its snakes,
They were like ropes six fathoms long.
Almighty God Most High
Created every kind of living thing.
It had sparrows as large as snowcocks,
And plane trees tall as misted towers,
And marshes spread in separate patches.
Ah, wondrous Ala-Köl—
It held creatures of extraordinary kinds.
When they entered Ala-Köl,
There also was one running with a rolling lope,
A creature called börsö.
Across that peopleless, empty plain,
Its flanks bulging outward,
Good heavens, there could be seen
The offspring of that börsö.
It held creatures of every kind,
No mortal had ever seen
The beasts of Tügöngür it held.
Ah, wondrous Ala-Köl—
Their slender tails quivered,
Their red heads bobbed,
And the geese rose in a boiling flight;
Wild fowl called noisily
Across the marshes where they lay.
There were marshes in separate patches,
And geese flying in scattered flocks.
Dark meadow grass and feather grass
Had grown into thick-headed herbage,
Sprang up again and filled the ground:
The season had turned to spring.
The ridges stood apart in folds;
From every side there roared
A cold, yellow wind.
It was a place where the cherished cap
With its blue-lynx trim shook in the gusts,
Where every heart opened freely,
And many fine men
Could live in delight.
At that time, there before them,
The young prince Semetey
Urged Buurul beneath him,
Made him plunge as though his master had died,
And cast the Akshunkar from his hand,
Setting it upon prey here,
Then setting it upon prey there.
He filled every saddle strap
With geese and ducks,
Hunted along this shore,
Then hunted along that one,
And loaded all his saddle straps
With geese and ducks;
What would not fit upon the straps
He hung from the crupper.
Your Akshunkar of Tengiz
Had talons of steel and a copper beak,
Its wingspan measured two fathoms;
Black-eyed, with blue-gray legs,
It let nothing it saw escape.
It was not sated by meat in bucketfuls,
And never ceased its striving;
It was not sated by meat in platterfuls.
It did not rustle when it spread its wings,
Nor startle the geese from the lake;
It did not rustle when it spread its tail,
Nor startle the swan from the lake.
He sent the falcon after it,
And Semetey drank his fill of joy.
Looming like Opol-Too,
Your mighty prince and sultan
Stumbled about, unable to find the swan.
At the edge of Ala-Köl,
Along the face of the reed beds,
From a great, noisy point,
At the tip of Kuu-Jeken,
There on Ala-Köl’s shore,
He saw a wondrous sight.
It moved with a resonant call,
Its voice unlike any swan’s;
It paced among the gray reeds,
Beating sand with its tail,
And beating the earth with its wings.
Its billowing feathers came apart;
When it called aloud,
Its deep voice could be heard.
Its neck was a fathom, its breast was straight;
It emerged from those reeds,
Appearing as large as a felt tent,
Grazing sedge and pulling grass,
Raising its head and pawing the earth.
Semetey, the brave son of Manas,
Looked closely and saw the swan.
On that dreadful, swaggering day,
Would your prince stand still?
He fell silent at the sight of the swan—
Had God struck the prince senseless?
To set the bird upon the swan,
And have it bring the swan down,
The poor prince grew eager,
And appealed to the Almighty.
He gripped the falcon on his arm
And drew it close against his side;
He touched Buurul beneath him
With his heel beneath the foreleg.
The young prince made Buurul
Step forward with long, rolling strides,
And trot with a rocking gait;
He sat holding the bird at an angle,
Bringing it into the proper position,
And made the falcon quiver,
Ready to remove its hood.
The tiger who loomed like a mountain
Prepared to cast it headlong,
And made the falcon ready.
Kulchoro and Kanchoro,
These two legacies left by bygone lions,
Came racing up together,
With Kulchoro crying urgently;
The two of them arrived.
Tall and broad-shouldered,
Kulchoro, son of Almambet,
Both a strongman and a lion,
Began speaking these words
To his elder kinsman:
“Kulchoro and Kanchoro—
We two were twin boys,
And souls who became companions to you.
If we choro died,
We were sons worth no more than dog hide;
While we remained alive,
We were servants worth no more than sheepskin.
Having girded his waist firmly,
The brave Semetey
Was born together
With his very self.
From Manas, who has gone to the next world,
Your dear mother Kanykey
Bore him, tearing open her womb;
Look here, tiger—
When were we ever sons of Manas?
My poor elder kinsman, hear my words.
Though we are servants, if we grow unruly,
While you, my khan and elder, are here,
And rage and swallow our anger,
If we set the bird upon the swan
